title: Validate the idea
summary: Pressure-test the idea before building: draft the problem hypothesis, pick the validation method the starting situation calls for (problem interviews, a lean MVP launch, concierge delivery, a product/market-fit survey, a pre-sale commitment, or a waitlist ad test), run it, and make the go/no-go call on the evidence.

parts.title: Draft problem hypothesis and target customer
parts.guidance: Describe the customer, the situation in which the problem occurs, the outcome they want, and how they handle it today. Separate what you have observed from assumptions about frequency, cost, urgency, or willingness to change. Pick the assumption that most threatens the idea and define what evidence would change your mind. Ask who wants this outcome so much they would use a rough first version from an unknown team (lore rule pg-deep-need-test); if no one fits that description, record it as the hypothesis's biggest open risk. That question should drive the first experiment and the decision you make from its results.

execution.rationale: Draft the problem hypothesis and the evidence that would change it from the supplied observations.

parts.title: Capture the hypothesis doc in Notion
parts.guidance: Put the hypothesis in the team's knowledge workspace, using Notion if selected. Include the customer and problem context, evidence already available, uncertain assumptions, and the question the next test will answer. Link research notes without widening access to participant information. Keep the starting version and append findings as the experiment runs, making changes to the hypothesis visible.

execution.rationale: Notion's page creation and block-append APIs save the hypothesis and add linked findings while retaining the starting version in the approved workspace.

parts.title: Choose the validation method
parts.guidance: Match the method to the founder's starting situation instead of defaulting to a favorite technique. The deciding facts: whether anything usable exists yet, whether target users are reachable and how desperate their problem is, whether the product carries a price a customer can commit to before it is built, and whether live usage data already exists. Prove the value hypothesis before spending anything on growth (lore rule griffin-value-before-growth), and run the smallest build-measure-learn loop that can answer the hypothesis's most threatening open question (lore rule ries-build-measure-learn). Record why the chosen method fits the situation, so a negative result reads on the idea rather than on the method.

options.title: Problem-interview sprint
options.summary: Interview people who encounter the problem when the main uncertainty is their current behavior, constraints, or buying context. Recruit against a defined customer profile and ask about real experiences before presenting the proposed solution. Compare workarounds, costs, decision-makers, and reasons someone would change. Compare contradictory accounts as well as common patterns. Distinguish predictions about future use from choices people have already made when deciding what to test next.
options.when: Cold start, including B2B / enterprise - no product and no audience yet, and the demand signal comes from conversations with named prospects, not anonymous clicks

parts.title: Draft the interview discussion guide
parts.guidance: Write questions that explore the uncertain assumptions in the hypothesis. Ask about the last time the problem occurred, what the person did, what it cost, and who influenced a purchase or change. Follow the Mom Test discipline: ask about the customer's life and past behavior, never pitch, and never ask whether they would buy (lore rule fitzpatrick-mom-test). Use neutral follow-ups and leave reactions to the proposed solution until after the account of actual behavior. Include consent and recording preferences at the start, and a note-taking format that separates the participant's words from the interviewer's interpretation.

execution.rationale: Draft neutral interview questions, consent prompts and an evidence-separated note template.

parts.title: Recruit 5-10 prospects matching the target customer
parts.guidance: Define screening criteria for the target role, experience, and problem context. Prepare a short invitation explaining the research purpose, expected participation, and any incentive, then agree the outreach list and message with the research lead before sending. The facts you need live outside the building: test the riskiest business-model assumptions directly with customers before building anything (lore rule blank-get-out-of-the-building). Recruit the planned initial group and note how each person qualified. Track gaps in the sample, such as only reaching existing friends or one customer segment, so those limits remain visible in the findings.

execution.rationale: Recruiting and qualification depend on the agreed prospect list and outreach channel.

parts.title: Run the interviews
parts.guidance: Confirm consent and recording preferences, then use the guide to explore specific incidents, workarounds, and decisions. Ask for examples when an answer becomes hypothetical, and avoid steering the participant toward the proposed solution. Capture their account separately from your interpretation. End by clarifying unresolved points and any follow-up they agree to, then finish the notes while the details are fresh and store them with the intended research access.

execution.rationale: Conducting live participant interviews requires the selected conversation and consent method.

parts.title: Synthesize notes into demand evidence
parts.guidance: Compare the interviews against the original assumptions, looking for repeated behavior, meaningful differences, and evidence that contradicts the idea. Group findings about the problem, current alternatives, urgency, buying authority, and barriers to change. Link each conclusion to its underlying notes. Expect the plan to change on contact: treat the synthesis as a search for a working business model, not a defense of the original plan (lore rule blank-no-plan-survives). Explain whose experience the sample represents and which questions remain open, then recommend a change to the hypothesis or a specific next test.

execution.rationale: Synthesize supplied interview notes into linked supporting and contradictory demand evidence.
The interview sprint includes participant conversations whose remote or in-person method is unspecified.

options.title: Lean MVP launch
options.summary: Ship the smallest real version of the product to users you can already reach, and let actual usage answer the hypothesis. Scope the first version to the single core use the hypothesis names, launch it before it feels finished, and iterate against what real users do rather than what they say. Judge the result on activation and return use within a bounded window, and treat silence as a result worth acting on.
options.when: A builder with reachable target users - the fastest honest signal is shipping a small real version and watching what people do with it

parts.title: Scope the MVP to the single core use
parts.guidance: Cut the plan to the one path that tests the hypothesis: hold the problem tightly and the solution loosely, and aim to build in weeks, not months (lore rule seibel-lean-mvp). Look for the 90/10 solution, the version that delivers most of the value for a fraction of the work (lore rule ralston-90-10-solution). Write down what is deliberately out of scope, so later feedback about missing edges is not mistaken for a verdict on the core.

execution.rationale: Write the bounded core-use specification and explicit exclusions for the hypothesis test.

parts.title: Build and launch the first version
parts.guidance: Build the scoped version and put it in front of real users. Launching version 1 is how you learn what you should have been building (lore rule pg-launch-fast), and a first release that feels slightly embarrassing usually means the timing is right (lore rule hoffman-embarrassing-first-launch). Describe what exists accurately, open a feedback channel from day one, and prefer shipping to polishing anything the hypothesis does not test.

execution.rationale: Building and launching the actual product depends on its chosen implementation and delivery environment.

parts.title: Measure usage against a bounded demand window
parts.guidance: Decide in advance what demand must look like and how long the launched version gets to show it; about a month is a workable bound for a first read (lore rule levels-one-month-market-test). Watch what users do after the first visit, separating activation and return use from raw signups. Bring the founder the behavior data with the strongest supporting and contradicting evidence, and a recommendation to iterate, narrow the audience, or stop.

execution.rationale: Analyze supplied activation and return-use data against the preselected demand window.
The MVP's actual product, launch interface and usage instrumentation are unspecified.

options.title: Concierge / manual MVP
options.summary: Deliver the proposed outcome manually for a small pilot group to learn what customers value and what the work involves. Agree the service boundary, customer inputs, payment if any, and what a useful result looks like before starting. Keep track of manual tasks and exceptions while delivering. Compare actual customer use, effort, and willingness to continue, then decide which parts deserve a product and which need a different approach.
options.when: A hair-on-fire market - users desperate enough to accept manual, imperfect delivery of the outcome today

parts.title: Recruit 2-3 pilot customers
parts.guidance: Find pilot customers who experience the problem now and can provide the inputs needed for manual delivery. Pick pilots by urgency: the hair-on-fire test asks for users whose problem is so dire they will try a half-baked first version (lore rule seibel-hair-on-fire-problems), and a few customers with a burning problem teach more than many with a passing annoyance (lore rule ralston-fire-bad-customers). Explain the proposed service, its limits, customer involvement, and any payment before inviting them to participate. Agree a concrete outcome each customer would find useful and who will provide access or feedback. Select the initial group with the pilot owner, distinguishing requirements shared across customers from individual exceptions.

execution.rationale: Pilot recruitment requires the actual customer outreach and agreement channel.

parts.title: Deliver the service manually end to end
parts.guidance: Carry out the agreed work using the customer's permitted inputs and access. Unscalable effort is the point at this stage: serve the pilots by hand (lore rule pg-do-things-that-dont-scale), and set each customer up on the spot instead of sending a link and waiting (lore rule pg-collison-installation). Note the manual tasks, decisions, exceptions, and customer handoffs as they occur, especially work that requires expertise or repeated clarification. Resolve scope changes with the pilot owner and customer before making new commitments. Deliver the result and ask the customer to use or assess it against the agreed outcome, capturing where the service still falls short.

execution.rationale: The customer outcome and required expertise or physical actions determine the pilot's delivery mechanism.

parts.title: Track effort, outcomes, and willingness to pay
parts.guidance: Compare the customer's use and feedback with the time, cost, and exceptions recorded during delivery. Look for work that repeats across pilots and for effort caused by one customer's unusual circumstances. Distinguish an expression of willingness to pay from an actual payment or agreement to continue. Use the findings to decide what should be automated, redesigned, priced differently, or tested with another customer.

execution.rationale: Compare recorded delivery effort, outcomes and continuation commitments across the pilot customers.
The pilot outcome and actual manual delivery tasks are unspecified.

options.title: Product/market-fit survey
options.summary: Put the Sean Ellis question, how would you feel if you could no longer use the product, to users who have genuinely experienced it, and measure the share who answer very disappointed. The score turns an argument about fit into a number the team can track across rounds, and the follow-up answers say which users to build for next. Survey new users each round and read the result against the benefit those users actually report.
options.when: The product is already live with active users - the open question is how disappointed they would be to lose it

parts.title: Define the surveyed population
parts.guidance: Select users who have experienced the core product at least twice in the last two weeks, and plan for about 40 respondents before reading the result as directional (lore rule vohra-survey-core-users). Pull the population from product analytics rather than memory, exclude teammates and test accounts, and record the selection criteria with the survey so later rounds stay comparable.

execution.rationale: The surveyed population must be pulled from the selected product analytics system and verified against its user records.

parts.title: Run the very-disappointed survey
parts.guidance: Ask how the user would feel if they could no longer use the product (very disappointed, somewhat disappointed, not disappointed), what type of person they think benefits most, what the main benefit is, and how the product could improve. The share answering very disappointed is the fit measure, with 40% as the bar before scaling (lore rule vohra-pmf-engine). Keep the survey short, send it while the product experience is recent, and store responses where the team can revisit the raw wording.

execution.rationale: The survey tool and delivery channel for collecting raw customer responses are unspecified.

parts.title: Segment responses and extract the signal
parts.guidance: Disregard feedback from users who would not be disappointed without the product, and split the somewhat-disappointed by whether the main benefit resonates with them, acting only on the feedback of those for whom it does (lore rule vohra-segment-by-main-benefit). Keep surveying new users, no user twice, and track the very-disappointed share over time as the core product metric (lore rule vohra-track-pmf-score-weekly). Bring the founder the score, the segments, and what holds the near-misses back.

execution.rationale: Response segmentation and scoring are local analysis, but this step also continues surveying new users and tracks repeated measurements. The survey delivery and deduplication mechanism is unspecified.
The survey distribution, collection and respondent-selection systems have not been selected.

options.title: Pre-sale commitment test
options.summary: For an enterprise idea the first commitment to seek is a signed letter of intent; for hardware or another physical product it is a refundable deposit. Test a preorder or refundable deposit only with a clear offer and a workable plan for handling customer funds. Explain what is being reserved, fulfillment uncertainty, cancellation terms, and how refunds work. Have the business owner and local adviser review the commitments before launch. Measure completed deposits and refunds, and keep someone responsible for customer questions and outstanding promises if the experiment changes direction or stops.
options.when: A priced product where a commitment is obtainable before building - an enterprise letter of intent, or a refundable deposit on a physical product

parts.title: Ask named buyers to commit before building
parts.guidance: Test an enterprise idea by trying to sell it first: ask the named buyer for a letter of intent saying they will purchase, before writing a line of code (lore rule altman-launch-or-loi-test). Commitments of money, time, or resources from real customers and partners reduce uncertainty more than any analysis (lore rule sarasvathy-stakeholder-precommitments). Record who committed, to what, and under which conditions; a polite expression of interest without a commitment counts as a no for this test.

execution.rationale: Seeking a buyer's actual commitment requires the agreed outreach and execution channel.

parts.title: Publish the preorder page
parts.guidance: Draft the preorder page with the item being reserved, the amount paid now, and the proposed delivery and cancellation terms. Have the business owner and the appropriate local adviser review the customer commitments before publication. Make fulfillment uncertainty visible and name a contact for questions. Check that checkout presents the same offer, and associate the page version with each order to support later fulfillment or refund questions.

references.title: FTC: Selling on the Internet, Prompt Delivery Rules

execution.rationale: The preorder page and checkout must be published and reconciled in the selected website and payment systems.

parts.title: Set up the refundable-deposit checkout
parts.guidance: Configure the deposit amount, currency, description, receipt, and refund process in the selected payment service. Check that the service permits the offer and that the company can return funds on the promised terms. Test payment and refund handling using the provider's supported method, then have the payment owner authorize live activation. Make deposits and outstanding refunds traceable to customers so stopping the experiment has a practical financial closeout path.

execution.rationale: Stripe is listed, but the deposit offer's permitted payment/refund setup and complete checkout test are not evidenced together.

parts.title: Measure deposit conversion and refund rate
parts.guidance: Reconcile completed deposits with payment records before calculating conversion from the relevant visitor or checkout population. Separate failed payments and internal tests from customer demand. Track cancellations, completed refunds, and outstanding requests, including why customers asked to leave. Compare those results with acquisition source and the offer shown, then bring the experiment owner both the demand findings and the work or funds needed to satisfy remaining customer obligations.

execution.rationale: Reconcile supplied deposit and refund records and calculate conversion while separating unresolved customer obligations.

references.title: FTC: Selling on the Internet, Prompt Delivery Rules

execution.rationale: The commitment test combines reviewed customer terms, a chosen payment route and fulfillment obligations that are not specified.

options.title: Waitlist + ad-spend test
options.summary: Use paid traffic and a waitlist to test response from a reachable target audience. Define the offer, audience, signup criteria, and spending limit before building the campaign. Obtain the budget owner's approval before paid launch, then connect the ad to a working signup page. Compare qualified responses and acquisition cost across the messages or audiences actually tested, checking traffic quality before attributing a weak result to the idea itself.
options.when: Consumer product - buy a small amount of traffic and measure real waitlist conversion

parts.title: Publish the waitlist page
parts.guidance: Build a page that explains the proposed outcome, who it is for, and what joining the waitlist provides. Write a clear offer and a single next action, decide which action counts as a useful response (a qualified signup or a request to talk), and state product availability accurately. Ask only for information needed for that follow-up and make its handling clear. Check the form, confirmation, and storage destination before publishing the experiment owner's agreed version. Keep the page aligned with the advertisement, and save its URL and offer version so campaign results can be compared with the message visitors actually saw.

execution.rationale: Lovable is listed, but the waitlist's live storage destination and publish-to-submission verification are not established.

parts.title: Launch a small paid ad campaign at the target audience
parts.guidance: Turn the chosen audience and offer into an accurate advertisement. Set the spending limit, targeting, destination, and stopping conditions, with a named person watching the campaign. Have the budget owner approve the spend before launch. Check that the live ad reaches the working signup page and that campaign identifiers survive the journey. Watch for unexpected spend, irrelevant traffic, or a broken destination before judging demand from the results.

execution.rationale: The selected advertising platform determines campaign activation, spend controls and live verification.

parts.title: Measure click-to-signup conversion
parts.guidance: Compare advertising clicks with page visits and completed signups, investigating discrepancies before calculating conversion. Remove internal submissions, duplicates, and obvious spam. Show the audience or message tested, sample size, spend, and qualified responses alongside the rate. Weigh conversion against depth of signal: a single passionate user of a crude prototype means more than a large waitlist (lore rule taggar-one-passionate-user-signal). Explain whether the result points to an audience problem, a weak offer, or a broken journey, and identify what another test would need to distinguish those explanations.

execution.rationale: Reconcile supplied click, visit and signup records and compute the qualified-response comparison.
The advertising platform, signup destination and audience measurement system are unspecified.
Recommend the validation method from the founder's starting facts and the most consequential untested assumption.

parts.title: Instrument signup analytics
parts.guidance: For an experiment with a digital signup or payment path, define the events needed to measure the response and exactly what triggers each event. Configure the chosen analytics within the company's agreed data and privacy limits. Make a test submission and inspect the recorded events, removing test traffic from results and noting tracking gaps. Interview-only tests and manual pilots can use their research or delivery records; add digital tracking only if it answers a question the experiment actually has.

execution.rationale: PostHog is listed, but the selected signup or payment triggers and event-inspection path are not established for this experiment.

parts.title: Run customer interviews
parts.guidance: Explore what the experiment's responses mean by talking with people who match the target customer. Ask about the problem, their current solution, and what would need to change for them to adopt the proposed offer. Reuse evidence from an interview sprint if that route already answered these questions, and recruit only for the gaps. Summarize what the conversations explain about observed behavior, keeping stated interest separate from a purchase or use decision.

execution.rationale: The follow-up customer conversations have no selected remote or in-person method.

parts.title: Analyze signups and interview notes
parts.guidance: Compare the experiment's offer versions, response data, interviews, and any delivery or payment results with the original success criteria. Resolve obvious data-quality problems and explain differences between customer segments. Separate conclusions supported by observed behavior from interpretations that need another test. Present the strongest supporting and contradictory evidence together, then identify the specific uncertainty that matters most to the founder's next decision.

execution.rationale: Analyze the supplied experiment results and interviews against the original criteria, preserving contradictory evidence.

parts.title: Go/no-go decision
parts.guidance: Decide whether to continue, change the hypothesis, run a narrower test, or stop, using the original criteria and the findings together. Commit only what the company can afford to lose at each step when sizing the next test (lore rule sarasvathy-affordable-loss), and budget for validation taking longer than expected rather than spending on growth before fit (lore rule griffin-premature-scaling). Explain what changed the founder's view and what the next commitment of time or money is intended to learn. Assign any promised customer follow-up and outstanding refunds before closing the test. Keep the decision with the experiment record so the next round begins from what the team has learned.

execution.rationale: The founder makes the next commitment of time or money; the decision and acceptance channel is unspecified.

links.when: The MVP has a digital signup or payment path to instrument.
The preorder page and checkout need conversion instrumentation.
The waitlist page needs click-to-signup instrumentation.
Interview evidence replaces digital conversion instrumentation.
Manual-delivery records replace digital conversion instrumentation.
The product's existing analytics already measure usage; interviews probe the survey segments.

metadata.supportReason: An agent can draft the hypothesis, propose the method that fits the starting situation, build the test assets, and analyze response data. Customer interviews, manual delivery, and the go/no-go decision are judgment work.
